#!/bin/bash

# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables in an unquoted
# assignment slot, then reference them only as "$VAR". Never interpolate
#  inside a quoted context - sanitize() (shlex.quote) wraps
# dangerous values in single quotes, which are literal (and command
# substitution stays active) inside a double-quoted or single-quoted slot.
KIND=deployments
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=boutique
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""

# Collapse multi-line jq expressions (LLMs sometimes write multi-line jq)
# Note: use $'\n' syntax instead of '\n' because Jinja2 interprets \n as literal newlines
JQ_FILTER='.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, env: [.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[]? | {name, value}], resources: .spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'
JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  exit 0
}

# The namespace becomes part of the raw API path, so anything other than a valid
# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."
fi

# Get the API path for the resource kind using kubectl
# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a
# grep regex - otherwise a kind like '.*' or 'a|b' would match the
# wrong resource.
CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)
# `kubectl api-resources` sorts by group name, so a CRD reusing a built-in
# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).

    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)

      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done

  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."
fi

else

fi

  fi

fi

#!/bin/bash

# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables in an unquoted
# assignment slot, then reference them only as "$VAR". Never interpolate
#  inside a quoted context - sanitize() (shlex.quote) wraps
# dangerous values in single quotes, which are literal (and command
# substitution stays active) inside a double-quoted or single-quoted slot.
KIND=nodes
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""

# Collapse multi-line jq expressions (LLMs sometimes write multi-line jq)
# Note: use $'\n' syntax instead of '\n' because Jinja2 interprets \n as literal newlines
JQ_FILTER='.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, conditions: [.status.conditions[] | select(.type!="MemoryPressure" and .type!="DiskPressure" and .type!="PIDPressure" and .type!="NetworkUnavailable") | {type, status, reason, message}], allocatable: .status.allocatable, capacity: .status.capacity}'
JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  exit 0
}

# The namespace becomes part of the raw API path, so anything other than a valid
# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."
fi

# Get the API path for the resource kind using kubectl
# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a
# grep regex - otherwise a kind like '.*' or 'a|b' would match the
# wrong resource.
CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)
# `kubectl api-resources` sorts by group name, so a CRD reusing a built-in
# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -c .)" -gt 1 ] && [[ "$API_INFO" != *" v1 "* ]]; then
  API_GROUPS=$(kubectl get --raw /apis 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.groups[].name' 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -z "$API_GROUPS" ]; then
    add_note "Several API groups serve '${KIND}' and server discovery (/apis) failed, so the first group listed by kubectl api-resources was used."
  fi
  for group in $API_GROUPS; do
    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)
    if [ -n "$match" ]; then
      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done
fi

if [ -z "$API_INFO" ]; then
  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Extract NAMESPACED value
if [[ "$API_INFO" == *" true "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."
fi

# Trim trailing spaces from prefix and collapse internal spaces
PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do
  ((FIELD_COUNT++))
done

RESOURCE_NAME="${PREFIX_FIELDS[0]}"
if [ $FIELD_COUNT -ge 2 ]; then
  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

if [ -z "$API_VERSION" ] || [ -z "$RESOURCE_NAME" ]; then
  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Build API path: namespaced kinds can be listed within one namespace;
# cluster-scoped kinds ignore the namespace (as kubectl does)
if [[ "$API_VERSION" == "v1" ]]; then
  API_BASE="/api/v1"
else
  API_BASE="/apis/${API_VERSION}"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && [ "$NAMESPACED" = "true" ]; then
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/namespaces/${SEL_NAMESPACE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
else
  if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
    add_note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${RESOURCE_NAME} is cluster-scoped."
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

SELECTOR_QUERY=""
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&labelSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_LABELS")"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&fieldSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_FIELDS")"
fi

SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg resource "$RESOURCE_NAME" --arg api_version "$API_VERSION" \
  --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
  '{resource: $resource, api_version: $api_version,
    namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
    label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
    field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')

# Process resources in chunks using API pagination
LIMIT=500
CONTINUE=""
TOTAL_MATCHES=0
ALL_MATCHES=""

while true; do
  QUERY="${API_PATH}?limit=${LIMIT}${SELECTOR_QUERY}"
  if [ -n "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    # continue tokens are base64 and may contain '+', '/' or '='
    QUERY="${QUERY}&continue=$(uri_encode "$CONTINUE")"
  fi

  OUTPUT=$(kubectl get --raw "$QUERY" 2>>"$err_file")
  exit_code=$?

  if [ $exit_code -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "kubectl get --raw failed for $QUERY."
  fi

  ITEMS_COUNT=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq '.items | length')

  MATCHES=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -c "$JQ_FILTER" 2>>"$err_file")
  jq_exit=$?
  if [ $jq_exit -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "jq expression failed."
  fi

  if [ "$ITEMS_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
    if [ -n "$MATCHES" ]; then
      if [ -z "$ALL_MATCHES" ]; then
        ALL_MATCHES="$MATCHES"
      else
        ALL_MATCHES="$ALL_MATCHES"$'\n'"$MATCHES"
      fi
      MATCH_COUNT=$(echo "$MATCHES" | grep -c . || true)
      TOTAL_MATCHES=$((TOTAL_MATCHES + MATCH_COUNT))
    fi
    PROCESSED=$((PROCESSED + ITEMS_COUNT))
  fi

  CONTINUE=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -r '.metadata.continue // empty')

  if [ -z "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    break
  fi
done

err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

# Output results as a JSON object with metadata. Results go through stdin, not --argjson:
# Linux caps a single argument at 128KB, so larger results failed with "Argument list too long".
printf '%s\n' "$ALL_MATCHES" | jq -s \
  --argjson total_items_processed "$PROCESSED" \
  --argjson matches_found "$TOTAL_MATCHES" \
  --arg stderr "$err_content" \
  --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
  --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
  '{total_items_processed: $total_items_processed, matches_found: $matches_found, results: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=

[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""

JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)

# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."

# wrong resource.

  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then

  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')

  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."

PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do

done

if [ $FIELD_COUNT -ge 2 ]; then
  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."

  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&labelSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_LABELS")"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&fieldSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_FIELDS")"
fi

SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg resource "$RESOURCE_NAME" --arg api_version "$API_VERSION" \
  --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
  '{resource: $resource, api_version: $api_version,

CONTINUE=""

ALL_MATCHES=""

  exit_code=$?

    fail "kubectl get --raw failed for $QUERY."
  fi

  ITEMS_COUNT=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq '.items | length')

  MATCHES=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -c "$JQ_FILTER" 2>>"$err_file")

  if [ $jq_exit -ne 0 ]; then

  --argjson total_items_processed "$PROCESSED" \
  --argjson matches_found "$TOTAL_MATCHES" \
  --arg stderr "$err_content" \
  --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
  --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
  '{total_items_processed: $total_items_processed, matches_found: $matches_found, results: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

# assignment slot, then reference them only as "$VAR". Never interpolate
#  inside a quoted context - sanitize() (shlex.quote) wraps

SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=

[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""

# Note: use $'\n' syntax instead of '\n' because Jinja2 interprets \n as literal newlines

JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  exit 0
}

# The namespace becomes part of the raw API path, so anything other than a valid
# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."
fi

# Get the API path for the resource kind using kubectl
# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a
# grep regex - otherwise a kind like '.*' or 'a|b' would match the
# wrong resource.
CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)

# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).

  if [ -z "$API_GROUPS" ]; then
    add_note "Several API groups serve '${KIND}' and server discovery (/apis) failed, so the first group listed by kubectl api-resources was used."
  fi
  for group in $API_GROUPS; do
    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)
    if [ -n "$match" ]; then
      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done
fi

if [ -z "$API_INFO" ]; then
  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."

PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do
  ((FIELD_COUNT++))
done

RESOURCE_NAME="${PREFIX_FIELDS[0]}"
if [ $FIELD_COUNT -ge 2 ]; then
  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

if [ -z "$API_VERSION" ] || [ -z "$RESOURCE_NAME" ]; then
  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# cluster-scoped kinds ignore the namespace (as kubectl does)

fi
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && [ "$NAMESPACED" = "true" ]; then
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/namespaces/${SEL_NAMESPACE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
else
  if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
    add_note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${RESOURCE_NAME} is cluster-scoped."
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

SELECTOR_QUERY=""
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&labelSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_LABELS")"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&fieldSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_FIELDS")"
fi

SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg resource "$RESOURCE_NAME" --arg api_version "$API_VERSION" \
  --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
  '{resource: $resource, api_version: $api_version,
    namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
    label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
    field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')

# Process resources in chunks using API pagination
LIMIT=500
CONTINUE=""
TOTAL_MATCHES=0
ALL_MATCHES=""

while true; do
  QUERY="${API_PATH}?limit=${LIMIT}${SELECTOR_QUERY}"
  if [ -n "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    # continue tokens are base64 and may contain '+', '/' or '='
    QUERY="${QUERY}&continue=$(uri_encode "$CONTINUE")"
  fi

  OUTPUT=$(kubectl get --raw "$QUERY" 2>>"$err_file")
  exit_code=$?

  if [ $exit_code -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "kubectl get --raw failed for $QUERY."
  fi

  ITEMS_COUNT=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq '.items | length')

  MATCHES=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -c "$JQ_FILTER" 2>>"$err_file")
  jq_exit=$?
  if [ $jq_exit -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "jq expression failed."
  fi

  if [ "$ITEMS_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
    if [ -n "$MATCHES" ]; then
      if [ -z "$ALL_MATCHES" ]; then
        ALL_MATCHES="$MATCHES"
      else
        ALL_MATCHES="$ALL_MATCHES"$'\n'"$MATCHES"

      TOTAL_MATCHES=$((TOTAL_MATCHES + MATCH_COUNT))
    fi
    PROCESSED=$((PROCESSED + ITEMS_COUNT))
  fi

  CONTINUE=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -r '.metadata.continue // empty')

  if [ -z "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    break
  fi
done

err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

# Output results as a JSON object with metadata. Results go through stdin, not --argjson:
# Linux caps a single argument at 128KB, so larger results failed with "Argument list too long".
printf '%s\n' "$ALL_MATCHES" | jq -s \
  --argjson total_items_processed "$PROCESSED" \
  --argjson matches_found "$TOTAL_MATCHES" \
  --arg stderr "$err_content" \
  --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
  --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
  '{total_items_processed: $total_items_processed, matches_found: $matches_found, results: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

#!/bin/bash
# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables (unquoted slot),
# then reference them only as "$VAR" - never interpolate 
# inside a quoted context. See kubernetes_jq_query for the rationale.
KIND=configmaps
CUSTOM_COLUMNS=NAME:.metadata.name,KEYS:.data
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=boutique
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
FILTER_PATTERN=kube-root-ca
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""
[ "$FILTER_PATTERN" = "None" ] && FILTER_PATTERN=""

# kubectl ignores -n for cluster-scoped kinds; say so instead of reporting a namespace that wasn't applied
NOTES='[]'
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  is_kind() { awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind || index($1, kind ".") == 1 {found = 1} END {exit !found}'; }
  if kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind \
    && ! kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind; then
    NOTES=$(jq -nc --arg note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${KIND} is cluster-scoped." '[$note]')
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
fi

SCOPE_ARGS=()
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-n "$SEL_NAMESPACE")
else
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--all-namespaces)
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-l "$SEL_LABELS")
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--field-selector "$SEL_FIELDS")
fi

err_file=$(mktemp)
output=$(kubectl get "$KIND" "${SCOPE_ARGS[@]}" -o custom-columns="$CUSTOM_COLUMNS" 2>"$err_file")
kubectl_exit=$?
err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

SCOPE='null'
if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
    '{namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
      label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
      field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')
fi

if [ $kubectl_exit -ne 0 ] || [ -z "$output" ]; then
  if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
    jq -n --arg stderr "$err_content" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
      '{count: 0, header: null, rows: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  else
    echo "=== STDERR ==="
    echo "$err_content"
    echo "=== ROWS ==="
    echo "=== COUNT ==="
    echo 0
  fi
  exit 0
fi

# Split header and data rows
header=$(echo "$output" | head -1)
if [ -n "$FILTER_PATTERN" ]; then
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2 | grep -E -- "$FILTER_PATTERN" || true)
else
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2)
fi

if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then
    count=$(echo "$data" | wc -l)
  else
    count=0
  fi
  # Rows go through stdin, not --argjson, so large tables don't hit "Argument list too long"
  printf '%s' "$data" | jq -R . | jq -s \
    --argjson count "$count" \
    --arg header "$header" \
    --arg stderr "$err_content" \
    --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
    '{count: $count, header: $header, rows: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
else
  echo "=== STDERR ==="
  echo "$err_content"
  echo "=== HEADER ==="
  echo "$header"
  echo "=== ROWS ==="
  echo "$data"
  echo "=== COUNT ==="
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then echo "$data" | wc -l; else echo 0; fi
fi

CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)
# `kubectl api-resources` sorts by group name, so a CRD reusing a built-in
# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -c .)" -gt 1 ] && [[ "$API_INFO" != *" v1 "* ]]; then
  API_GROUPS=$(kubectl get --raw /apis 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.groups[].name' 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -z "$API_GROUPS" ]; then
    add_note "Several API groups serve '${KIND}' and server discovery (/apis) failed, so the first group listed by kubectl api-resources was used."
  fi
  for group in $API_GROUPS; do
    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)
    if [ -n "$match" ]; then
      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done
fi

if [ -z "$API_INFO" ]; then
  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Extract NAMESPACED value
if [[ "$API_INFO" == *" true "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."
fi

# Trim trailing spaces from prefix and collapse internal spaces
PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do
  ((FIELD_COUNT++))
done

RESOURCE_NAME="${PREFIX_FIELDS[0]}"
if [ $FIELD_COUNT -ge 2 ]; then
  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

if [ -z "$API_VERSION" ] || [ -z "$RESOURCE_NAME" ]; then
  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Build API path: namespaced kinds can be listed within one namespace;
# cluster-scoped kinds ignore the namespace (as kubectl does)
if [[ "$API_VERSION" == "v1" ]]; then
  API_BASE="/api/v1"
else
  API_BASE="/apis/${API_VERSION}"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && [ "$NAMESPACED" = "true" ]; then
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/namespaces/${SEL_NAMESPACE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
else
  if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
    add_note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${RESOURCE_NAME} is cluster-scoped."
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

SELECTOR_QUERY=""
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&labelSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_LABELS")"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&fieldSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_FIELDS")"
fi

SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg resource "$RESOURCE_NAME" --arg api_version "$API_VERSION" \
  --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
  '{resource: $resource, api_version: $api_version,
    namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
    label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
    field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')

# Process resources in chunks using API pagination
LIMIT=500
CONTINUE=""
TOTAL_MATCHES=0
ALL_MATCHES=""

while true; do
  QUERY="${API_PATH}?limit=${LIMIT}${SELECTOR_QUERY}"
  if [ -n "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    # continue tokens are base64 and may contain '+', '/' or '='
    QUERY="${QUERY}&continue=$(uri_encode "$CONTINUE")"
  fi

  OUTPUT=$(kubectl get --raw "$QUERY" 2>>"$err_file")
  exit_code=$?

  if [ $exit_code -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "kubectl get --raw failed for $QUERY."
  fi

  ITEMS_COUNT=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq '.items | length')

  MATCHES=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -c "$JQ_FILTER" 2>>"$err_file")
  jq_exit=$?
  if [ $jq_exit -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "jq expression failed."
  fi

  if [ "$ITEMS_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
    if [ -n "$MATCHES" ]; then
      if [ -z "$ALL_MATCHES" ]; then
        ALL_MATCHES="$MATCHES"
      else
        ALL_MATCHES="$ALL_MATCHES"$'\n'"$MATCHES"
      fi
      MATCH_COUNT=$(echo "$MATCHES" | grep -c . || true)
      TOTAL_MATCHES=$((TOTAL_MATCHES + MATCH_COUNT))
    fi
    PROCESSED=$((PROCESSED + ITEMS_COUNT))
  fi

  CONTINUE=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -r '.metadata.continue // empty')

  if [ -z "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    break
  fi
done

err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

# Output results as a JSON object with metadata. Results go through stdin, not --argjson:
# Linux caps a single argument at 128KB, so larger results failed with "Argument list too long".
printf '%s\n' "$ALL_MATCHES" | jq -s \
  --argjson total_items_processed "$PROCESSED" \
  --argjson matches_found "$TOTAL_MATCHES" \
  --arg stderr "$err_content" \
  --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
  --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
  '{total_items_processed: $total_items_processed, matches_found: $matches_found, results: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

These are mutually exclusive — never add "or the user may not exist" to an authentication failure.

A node condition does not tell you which pods it hit; a failing dependency does not tell you which of its clients broke; an unhealthy shared component does not mean its consumers are unhealthy. Check each entity before you name it, or do not name it — sampling a workload's replicas characterizes the WORKLOAD, so attribute what you found to it rather than to replicas you did not look at.

A pod that is 5 minutes old on a node that had trouble 5 minutes ago was not necessarily evicted — check what created it. Coincidence in time is not causation, and "also affected" is a claim that needs its own evidence.

Every line here quotes the exact reason token that proves it, in parentheses: `Evicted`, `OOMKilled`, `BackOff`, `Failed`, `Unhealthy` on a long-running pod, an error log line. If you cannot quote such a token for that entity, it does not go here — `SuccessfulDelete`, `SuccessfulCreate`, `Scheduled`, `Started` and a probe miss at startup are not among them. A recreation, restart or probe miss inside the window is never enough on its own, whatever sub-label you give it; **Checked, healthy** — you looked and found nothing wrong; **Changed during the window for another reason** — it restarted, was recreated or errored, and you name what did it (a controller rollout, a scheduled job, an operator, a probe at startup) and how you know; **Not checked**. messages.reasoning_content:
Excellent! The loadgenerator stats confirm:
- GET / : 24ms avg, 18 med — fast
- GET /cart: 361 avg, 410 med — slow
- POST /cart: 372 avg, 420 med — slow
- GET /product/*: ~360 avg, 410 med — slow
- POST /setCurrency: 27ms — fast
- POST /cart/checkout: 103 avg, med 4 — failing (26/39, old data)

So cart page and product page are slow, homepage fast. But this data appears to be cumulative from start (includes pre-fix failures). Interesting: /cart AND /product are slow, homepage fast.

What differs? Homepage (home handler) calls: getCurrencies, getProducts, getCart, chooseAd. Cart page calls: getCurrencies, getCart, getRecommendations, getShippingQuote, getShippingCost... Product page: getProduct, getCurrencies, getRecommendations, getAd.

Common slow calls: recommendations? But homepage doesn't call recommendations. Hmm, cart page calls recommendations in the demo (`getRecommendations` in viewCartHandler). Product page also. Homepage doesn't.

That's consistent with recommendationservice being the culprit → my round-1 hypothesis. But raising CPU limit to 1 did not help. Log timestamps show recommendation receives requests with ~1s granularity, at like 2-4 per second... no indication of slow handling.

Wait, but also both cart and product pages call getShippingQuote (cart page) — homepage doesn't. Product page doesn't call shipping. So the common one is recommendations.

Alternatively, the delay could be in frontend's own handler but not the home handler... The cart page also calls currencyservice conversions (getShippingCost -> ConvertCurrency), and product page calls convertCurrency for the product price and recommendations' prices. Homepage also calls getCurrencies (ListCurrencies, cheap) and convertCurrency? In the demo home handler converts product prices? Actually home handler: `getCurrencies`, `getProducts`, `getCart`, then `convertCurrency` for each product price. Hmm, home does call convertCurrency per product. So currency isn't the difference.

So recommendation is the differentiator. But we raised CPU — no improvement. Maybe there's another issue in recommendationservice: e.g., its call to productcatalogservice (ListProducts) is slow. recommendationservice calls productcatalogservice.ListProducts on every ListRecommendations!

So maybe productcatalogservice is slow. But homepage calls productcatalogservice.ListProducts (getProducts) too and homepage is 24ms — so productcatalog is fast.

Hmm. So both cart and product pages slow, homepage fast: the difference is recommendation call. But CPU limit was already raised.

Wait — is the recommendation call actually slow? Maybe the frontend has a wrong RECOMMENDATION_SERVICE_ADDR... it's recommendationservice:8080 correct.

Alternative difference: cart page and product page → the "cart" size? Both call getCart. Homepage also calls getCart.

Hmm, what about `/setCurrency` fast (27ms) — that just sets cookie.

Let me reconsider: Maybe latency ~410ms comes from the frontend pods' own CPU limit 200m and heavy rendering of product/cart pages? Hmm, thresholds 180ms.

Let's look for hard evidence rather than guessing. Check frontend logs — the demo frontend doesn't log durations. But we can look at cartservice logs (has timings?). Let's check other services' logs for latency. productcatalogservice logs may log "GetProduct" etc.

Better: measure per-service by looking at logs sequence? Hmm.

Another approach: check CPU throttling from node cgroup files — no exec tool.

Hmm, but maybe we can check pod's cgroup via... no.

What about the kubelet stats? Not accessible.

Let me consider the recommendation hypothesis more carefully. The Python recommendation service: ListRecommendations calls productcatalogservice.ListProducts each time with a gRPC connection created per call? In v0.10.x sample, recommendationservice creates a new grpc channel per request? Something like: in `server.py`, `with make_channel(...)`? Actually there is a known behavior: recommendationservice re-creates channel each request in some versions... That would add DNS resolution time per call. If DNS is slow (e.g., ndots search path delays), ~400ms.

Wait! Interesting: base latency ~410ms exists on product & cart pages. If recommendationservice makes a per-request gRPC dial to productcatalogservice, DNS resolution could add latency. Also, frontend makes connection per request...

Let's measure recommendation service internal time indirectly: send? We can't. But logs: recommendationservice logs [Recv ListRecommendations] at request time. Compare frontend request start? Not logged.

Alternative: check if there's a per-request log in productcatalogservice — the Go sample logs nothing per request normally.

Hmm, what about checking the CPU limits for other services? All 200m which is the demo default (demo uses 200m for most). Only recommendationservice default is 200m/100m too... The reference demo values: recommendationservice cpu limit 200m, request 100m. That's normal, so not a fault.

So what is injected? The scenario: two faults maybe. Round1 found checkout env misconfig (definitely injected). The second fault is the latency one. Where?

Look at things that differ from upstream defaults:
- frontend memory limit 128Mi (default 128Mi ok)
- redis-cart cpu limit 125m (default 200m? In demo, redis-cart limits cpu 200m... Actually demo: redis-cart resources limits cpu 200m memory 256Mi? Hmm.)
- productcatalogservice 200m (demo default 200m)
- adservice 300m (demo default 300m)
- cartservice 300m (default 300m)
- emailservice 200m, paymentservice 200m, currencyservice 200m, shippingservice 200m, checkout 200m. These match demo defaults.

So resources are default except recommendationservice was modified by me.

Hmm, so what else? Maybe the injected fault is a service targetPort mismatch? All targetPorts look correct. Service selectors all correct.

What about a Service with wrong port for `frontend-external`? Port 80 → 8080, correct.

Wait, maybe the latency is caused by productcatalogservice having an extra env like EXTRA_LATENCY? In the demo, there's no such thing... but there IS an artificial latency feature in some versions: productcatalogservice supports `EXTRA_LATENCY` env var! Yes! In microservices-demo, productcatalogservice (Go) reads env `EXTRA_LATENCY` and sleeps. Let me recall: In productcatalogservice, there's `extraLatency` parsed from env "EXTRA_LATENCY" — yes, in the demo there is `EXTRA_LATENCY` support in productcatalogservice (used for demos of latency). Let me check the env of productcatalogservice: only PORT, DISABLE_PROFILER. So not set there.

But recommendationservice? No.

Hmm, what other env could cause latency... Let's check all deployments more thoroughly for envFrom, and check configmaps, and check the frontend pod spec fully (including any initContainers, sidecars). Also check for a second container.

Also: could the latency come from the frontend resolving DNS? Homepage also does.

Hmm wait. Reconsider the loadgen data: GET / is 24ms avg with only 44 requests vs product pages ~60 each and cart 118. The "/" home handler in frontend v0.10.3: it doesn't call recommendation. The product page calls recommendation (4 recommendations), cart page calls recommendation too.

So recommendation is the only common differentiator. Since CPU limit increase didn't help, maybe the issue is elsewhere in recommendationservice's path: e.g. its call to productcatalogservice creates a new channel per request (in v0.10.3, recommendationservice gets a cached stub — `self.product_catalog_stub` created at init).

Alternatively, recommendationservice is not the delay; maybe the delay is in frontend's `getRecommendations` because the frontend dials recommendationservice per request with DNS. But homepage dials other services per request too.

Hmm, what about a NetworkPolicy delaying? no.

Let's check the recommendationservice logs for a gap: each ListRecommendations arrival vs. next. If the service were slow, arrivals would still be arriving (concurrent). The arrival rate ~2-4/s.

Let's check recommendation pod's CPU limits now = 1; if CPU were the issue, latency would have dropped. Confirmed not CPU.

Next possibility: the delay is in the AD service call on product pages? Product page calls getAd as well. Cart page doesn't call ad. So no.

So: recommendation. What in recommendation could take 400ms? It calls productcatalogservice ListProducts. Product page also calls productcatalog GetProduct (fast, since / is fast with ListProducts). Hmm, that argues productcatalog is fast.

Unless... recommendationservice's Python has `DISABLE_PROFILER=1` but has OpenTelemetry exporting? No.

Wait — maybe recommendationservice has a wrong PRODUCT_CATALOG_SERVICE_ADDR? It's productcatalogservice:3550 ✓.

Hmm, is 410ms maybe a DNS timeout for the recommendation service's dialing? Python grpc dial to "productcatalogservice:3550" resolves once at startup.

Let me look at the actual latency distribution: min 8-10ms, median 410, max 440 (mostly 439-458). So most requests are ~410 and some are ~8-10ms. That's a bimodal pattern — like a coin flip! 60% slow at ~410ms, 40% fast. That suggests two replicas or two code paths, or a caching behavior: e.g., some requests hit a cache, others don't.

Bimodal: e.g., a DNS lookup with a cache TTL, or an iptables round-robin between endpoints. But there's only 1 replica of each service.

Actually maybe it's the home page (fast) vs product/cart (slow) computed in aggregate? No, per-endpoint medians: /cart median 410, product pages median 410, min 8-9ms. So within the same endpoint, some requests are 8ms and some 410ms. Interesting! So it's request-level variation, not endpoint-level.

Wait but "Min 8, Med 410, Max 458" — could be the median 410 with 60% slow. So per request, either fast (8-10ms) or +400ms. Bimodal per request.

That smells like: a service call that's sometimes fast, sometimes slow — e.g., DNS resolution with a mix, or a load-balancing between two endpoints where one is slow (but 1 replica each), or a periodic/lazy reconnection, or a cache miss path (e.g., recommendationservice's product catalog call with a cache).

Hmm, another thought: gRPC keepalive/channel idle. In the frontend, each incoming request creates a new gRPC connection to each backend (mustConnGRPC per request). Then the target service may need to establish... hmm that's still fast normally.

Bimodal delay ~400ms constant = suspiciously like DNS. If a pod's resolv.conf has options ndots:5 and search domains, resolving "recommendationservice" (a name with no dots) tries search paths. glibc DNS: sends A and AAAA queries in parallel to first nameserver; if first nameserver times out after 5s... no.

But 400ms? Hmm.

Alternatively ~410ms could be TCP connection establishment to a nonexistent/blackholed endpoint? No, that'd be seconds.

Wait — what if this is gRPC retry against a dead endpoint? Let me reconsider adservice: ads calls failed with connection refused up to 16:56. Now adservice is ready. But maybe adservice's Service has an endpoint that's... no.

New idea: check whether the loadgenerator data is cumulative since pod start (16:55). Then the "fast" min 8ms entries might be from before/after failures. Median from all requests since start ~410. Consistent.

Let's find harder evidence: check productcatalogservice / recommendationservice logs at timestamps and correlate with frontend request logs. The frontend logs the request start? It logs errors only. Hmm, we can use request completion? Not logged.

Alternatively check cartservice logs — the .NET cart service logs? It logs "GetCartAsync called with userId=..." maybe with timings. Let's check cartservice and currencyservice logs.

Another way: maybe there's a "frontend" deployment with 2 containers or a sidecar injecting latency? Let's check the full pod spec of frontend and recommendation.

Also check configmaps in the namespace (maybe a chaos config), and check for other resource kinds: networkpolicies, virtualservices, and any CRDs.

Let's do these.

messages.reasoning_content:
Note oddity: recommendation single-id recvs total 11 since pod start (~6 min), with timestamps 17:03:24, 17:03:43, 17:04:00, ... all for '2ZYFJ3GM2N'! All 11 single-id recvs are for the SAME product 2ZYFJ3GM2N. That's bizarre — unless... the product page's recommendation call is only logged for one product? No wait — maybe the recommendation service logs are sampled/deduplicated? Hmm.

Look: the earlier single-id log list showed 4 entries, all '2ZYFJ3GM2N'. Now latest 3 also 2ZYFJ3GM2N. So all single-id recvs are for product 2ZYFJ3GM2N. Interesting!!! But /product/2ZYFJ3GM2N views are only ~60 in the whole loadgen table...

Hmm, that suggests something is calling ListRecommendations with ['2ZYFJ3GM2N'] every ~20 seconds regardless of frontend traffic. That smells like a *probe/health check* or a background task. Or a retry loop.

Hmm, or the log *source* is deduplicating? The tool might dedupe identical lines?! Since all these single-id lines would be identical except the timestamp, maybe the tool deduplicates by content... but timestamps differ. Hmm.

I wonder if the log tool samples lines. The counts: "Total logs found before filtering: 622" for rec (pod started 17:01:06 → 17:07:10 = 364s). 622-5 = 617 ListRecommendations in 364s = 1.7/s. And frontend product views: 794 in the -330s window's buffer (5781 lines). If the frontend buffer is 5781 lines covering... at ~4 lines/request → 1445 requests over 330s = 4.4 req/s. Hmm, but user-side says 2.9 req/s. 

Frontend product views 794 over 330s = 2.4/s. Cart views 422 (earlier, over a similar buffer) hmm.

If product views = 2.4/s and cart views ~1.3/s, total cart+product = 3.7/s, but recommendation only gets 1.7/s. So ~half of cart/product page views don't produce a rec call?!

And single-id recvs = 11 in 364s (0.03/s) vs product views 2.4/s. So product pages' rec calls are essentially NOT reaching the service, but 1.7/s of 5-id calls do arrive. So the 5-id calls aren't from cart pages either (cart pages ~1.3/s?).

Hmm! What if the frontend's recommendation requests go to... wait. Something is inconsistent. Let me hypothesize: **the frontend's recommendation calls are slow (400ms)** and mostly *time out*? No errors logged.

Alternatively, the loadgen's product page views are being served from a cache? no.

Hmm, wait. Maybe the frontend log buffer covers a much longer window than 330s (e.g., the tool's 5781 lines is a hard cap over a longer period). If the frontend buffer covers, say, 700s, then product views = 794/700 = 1.1/s, cart = 0.6/s, total 1.7/s = matches recommendation's 1.7/s!! And single-id recvs 11 in 364s remain anomalous (but maybe the rec buffer covers a different span, e.g. 622 logs at 1.7/s = 364s exactly since pod start — reliable).

So product pages calling rec with a single id: expected ~0.7/s = 250 in 364s, observed 11. Still anomalous.

Unless the product page's recommendation request includes more than one id... OH WAIT. Maybe this demo's frontend productHandler passes `[]string{p.GetId()}` — but the *recommendation* service log for a *single* id is "product_ids=['2ZYFJ3GM2N']" — and we see ~11 of those (all for 2ZYFJ3GM2N), plus ~600 multi-id ones. Hmm, if product pages (1/s) passed single ids, we'd see ~360 single-id lines with various ids. We see 11, all the same id.

This strongly suggests the log tool *deduplicates similar lines* or *samples*. The counts "Total logs found: 622" vs filter matched 11 seems reliable though...

Alternatively the rec service logs are being sampled by the log backend (e.g., 1% sampling?). If the backend samples, all my correlation attempts are garbage.

Given: total rec logs 622 over 364s at 1.7/s. If sampling were on, that'd be fewer. So no sampling.

Hmm, so 11 single-id calls, ALL for the same product 2ZYFJ3GM2N. What calls recommendations with exactly 2ZYFJ3GM2N repeatedly, ~every 20s? Hmm, that's like a *user* whose cart has one item... The loadgen's cart page passes the cart's item ids — a session with one item '2ZYFJ3GM2N' would produce single-id cart page calls! And if that user's cart stays 1 item... but then we'd see single-id calls for other products too when other sessions have 1-item carts.

Honestly, cart pages with a single item are plausible: sessions that just added one item and view the cart. So single-id = 1-item cart page. And product page recommendation calls... would be 1-id too, indistinguishable. So if product pages called rec, there'd be MANY single-id recvs (2.4/s). We observe 0.03/s. CONCLUSION: **the frontend's product page is NOT calling recommendationservice** (or its calls don't arrive).

But then why is the product page slow?

Unless... hmm! What if the product page's recommendation call FAILS immediately (e.g., connection error) and the frontend logs a warning "failed to get recommendations" which I filtered out earlier? Let me check for that explicitly! Earlier I filtered frontend logs with 'duration|latency|slow|error|warn' over 600s and saw only ads errors + checkout errors. Hmm, but maybe the rec error message doesn't contain those words... In the frontend code:
```go
	log.WithField("error", err).Warn("failed to retrieve recommendations")
```
That contains "failed" and "warn" — my filter had 'error|warn' so it would match. It didn't appear. Hmm, but the log buffer for the frontend may be truncated (5781 lines cap) — the earlier scan hit its own 120-line limit? It said "Matched: 57 logs (1.5% of total)" and showed all 57. So no rec warnings in the frontend buffer.

So product pages don't error on rec.

I'm stuck on reconciling. Let me consider that the frontend's *product page* uses a **different** flow: In v0.10.3 productHandler:

```go
func (fe *frontendServer) productHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	...
	p, err := fe.getProduct(r.Context(), id)
	currencies, err := fe.getCurrencies(r.Context())
	cart, err := fe.getCart(r.Context(), sessionID(r))
	price, err := fe.convertCurrency(r.Context(), p.GetPriceUsd(), currentCurrency(r))
	recommendations, err := fe.getRecommendations(r.Context(), sessionID(r), []string{id})
```
Hmm — I *believe* this. 

Whereas maybe in v0.10.3, getRecommendations is called with `[]string{}`?? If ProductIds is empty, the recommendation service would still log product_ids=[] (which my regex wouldn't match, and the "5-id" lines wouldn't be these). Are there lines with `product_ids=[]`? Let me check for an empty list! filter "product_ids=\[\]". And what about the 5-id lines: those would be cart pages with 5 items (plausible, most carts have 5 items? the loadgen adds 1 item per session mostly...). Hmm, carts with 5 items exist since logs show 5 ids commonly.

Let's check for `product_ids=[]` — maybe that's the bulk! Then product pages call rec with an empty list, and rec returns ... and logs. Let's check. And also count "product_ids=\[\]," patterns.

Actually the vast majority of rec logs ARE 5-id and 4-id ones. Whatever.

Let me pivot decisively. I've got limited value from more log spelunking. Time to reason about the most probable fixable fault, and use the remaining actions wisely.

Wait. Actually — hold on! A new idea just struck me: **productcatalogservice's `GetProduct` for the recommendation flow**... no.

Better: What about the **`frontend` reading `products.json` from a mounted ConfigMap**? no.

Hmm, what about **adservice** latency? Product page calls ads; home calls ads... Wait, does home really call ads in v0.10.3? The earlier frontend error at 16:55:56.039 for path "/product/LS4PSXUNUM" and 16:55:55.6 for "/" — yes both. OK.

Alright. Let me consider the possibility that the frontend product page's 400ms comes from `fe.getRecommendations` where the *connection* is fine and the rec service responds in 5ms — and the extra 400ms comes from... the frontend waiting for something else. What else? Nothing.

Hmm, hmm. Unless the 400ms is not in the handler at all but in the frontend's *HTTP response write* — e.g., the handler completes in 5ms but `took_ms` measured 400ms... no, took_ms is measured around the handler.

Let's look at the cart page and product page: BOTH ~400ms, and both include "recommendations" section. Home 11ms.

Ugh, I keep coming back. Fine: assume it's the recommendation RPC and that it takes ~390ms round trip. Why? Because of the *Python server's connection handling*: If the frontend (Go gRPC client) opened a NEW TCP connection per RPC... 

AH WAIT. Big realization! What if the recommendationservice pod **is not the pod that the frontend connects to**... no, endpoints correct.

What if the **frontend's gRPC connection to recommendationservice is broken and every RPC triggers a reconnect**: gRPC Go in "TRANSIENT_FAILURE" backoff → each RPC would fail immediately, not 400ms. But if the connection is *half-open*, the RPC write succeeds silently, and the client waits for a response that never comes until **keepalive timeout**... gRPC's default keepalive for clients is disabled; but the RPC would hang forever, not 400ms.

400ms is just so specific. Combined with the fact that a *fresh pod* (17:01:04) didn't change it, and health/all configs fine...

New thought: maybe the 400ms comes from the **Node's network stack / CNI** (e.g., conntrack full, or a duplicated iptables rule) — affects all pods though.

Hmm, is 400ms maybe consistent with **DNS AAAA lookup timeout**? If the resolver sends an AAAA query to a server that doesn't respond, some resolvers wait ~400-500ms?? CoreDNS responds instantly with NODATA. But if a search domain is unreachable... 

WHO does DNS per request? Maybe the *recommendation* service DOES create a channel per request (Python!). Let me settle this by checking the v0.10.3 source. I can't access the internet (internet tool disabled). Hmm.

Wait, but if rec created a channel per request, DNS would be needed per request. With a slow DNS (~390ms), each ListRecommendations takes ~400ms. And the frontend's Go services resolve only at startup → fine. The recv log is written at request arrival (before the catalog call) → consistent with recv≈start. Everything fits EXCEPT the anomaly of product-page single-id counts (which might just be my misreading of logs/sampling).

But WHY would DNS be slow? Hmm, because CoreDNS is unhealthy? Then the *other* pods would fail at startup (they'd never resolve); they resolved fine at startup (all worked initially). A DNS degradation *after* startup would only affect per-request resolvers = recommendationservice! THIS FITS PERFECTLY.

And how does that get fixed with the allowed ops? Restart recommendationservice wouldn't fix DNS. Hmm. Unless... it's a **conntrack/NAT issue**: DNS UDP packets from pods getting dropped due to conntrack table full on the node — that would clear over time or need a node-level fix (not in our ops).

Hmm. But wait — if DNS were the problem, the DNS lookups would be per-request only if the channel is per-request. And the delay would be ~resolver timeout (typically 5s, or 2 attempts × ...). 400ms is short for a DNS timeout.

Hmm, what if it's not DNS but **TCP connect delay due to the pod's outbound NAT**?

I think I need a different discriminator: does the slowness scale with the number of recommendation calls per page? Product page: 1 rec call → 400ms. Cart page: 1 rec call → 415ms. Both ~equal. Consistent with a single ~400ms rec call.

Fine. So one rec call = ~400ms.

Decision: The realistic next actions:
1. `restart recommendationservice` — cheap, tests whether a fresh pod (with fresh DNS/NAT state and fresh channels) helps. Note: it was already recreated at 17:01:04 and latency persisted → a restart alone probably won't help. But it did happen 5 min ago... and latency persisted, so restart = no-op. Skip? Given max 6 actions, including it costs little but wastes budget. Hmm.

2. `scale recommendationservice 2` — halves per-pod load; if the delay is per-pod (e.g., serialization, in-pod network state), the second pod may be healthy! Interesting: if the cause is pod-local (e.g., that pod's DNS/conntrack state), a new pod from scaling would be fine and ~50% of requests would be fast. That's a genuinely useful diagnostic AND potential mitigation. Even better: scale to 3.

Wait, but with 1 rec replica and 50/50... hmm.

3. Also consider `set_cpu_limit recommendationservice 2` — no, proven irrelevant.

Alternatively, if the real cause is on the *catalog* side for recommendation's path... 

Hmm, and what about **productcatalogservice**: if the rec service's ListProducts is slow due to catalog, then GetProduct from the frontend would also be slow → product page's getProduct is fast (page ends up 400ms total, and POST /cart with getProduct = 1ms). So catalog is fast. 

OK so rec's 400ms is not its catalog call... unless the rec→catalog connection is bad specifically.

Hmm, what if the rec pod's *egress* is broken and its ListProducts RPC hangs/retries? Then rec would log ... no completion logs.

Given the ambiguity, a smart action set:
- scale recommendationservice to 2 (new pod; distributes load; if the old pod's network state is bad, ~half the traffic gets fast)

Hmm, but hold on: is there a chance the second fault isn't rec at all, and my round-1 fix (CPU) was wrong on the target? Let's sanity-check the ratio: 60.4% before → 64.8% after. Requests >180ms: cart+product ≈ 60-65% of traffic. Matches.

Alternatively the slow paths might be cart+product because of... the cart page and product page both render **the ads + recommendations**... 

You know what? Let me test the recommendation hypothesis EMPIRICALLY using an allowed action: `scale recommendationservice 2` — if latency halves for rec calls, we learn; if unchanged, rec isn't the bottleneck. But scaling doesn't *remove* rec calls from the path, so latency stays ~400 if per-request.

Better test: there's no way to remove rec from the path (can't edit frontend env to bypass → actually we CAN: `unset_env frontend RECOMMENDATION_SERVICE_ADDR`! If the env var is empty, the frontend's getRecommendations fails fast (logs warning) and the page renders without recommendations — a legit diagnostic: if /product and /cart become fast, rec is confirmed as the 400ms source. But is that an acceptable "fix"? It degrades functionality (no recommendations) — not a good user-facing fix, though it would isolate. Hmm, it's reversible and it's a diagnostic. But it's ugly for a "fix" request. 

Alternatively `set_env frontend RECOMMENDATION_SERVICE_ADDR recommendationservice:8080` — no change.

Hmm, what about the reverse: since recommendation receives requests *immediately* (recv ≈ start), the delay is inside the recommendation service after receipt. The most likely *config-fixable* thing inside is CPU. Already raised to 1 — no effect. What if the pod is limited by... memory? no.

Hmm, one more: maybe the recommendation service's *response* is delayed by its `ThreadPoolExecutor` — if the service handles only 10 concurrent... 1.7/s is low.

So the only remaining lever: pod-local transient state → restart. But the pod is 6 min old (fresh) and slow from the start. So pod-local state is ruled out!! A restart produces the same.

Therefore: something *external* to the rec pod: node network/DNS, or a sidecar-less injection.

Hmm... unless the fault IS in the rec's *gRPC channel keepalive* toward productcatalog: on a fresh pod the channel is created at startup; if the *node's* conntrack entry for that 5-tuple gets dropped after some idle... but requests are 1.7/s, no idling.

Hmm hold on, WAIT. What about the **DNS cluster domain search path**? If pod resolv.conf has `ndots:5` and the app dials "productcatalogservice:3550" (no dots) → the resolver tries search domains sequentially: productcatalogservice.boutique.svc.cluster.local (hit). Fine.

Let me examine one more time whether there's any *other* pod-level anomaly: rec's memory limit 450Mi, requests 220Mi. Python process RSS? unknown.

I'm now fairly convinced the rec processing delay is due to something we can't see from K8s objects. But benchmarks usually inject fixable faults...

Let me re-derive from the numbers whether the 400ms is *behind* the frontend at all. Evidence: frontend handler took_ms = 400ms for /cart and /product, 11-38ms for / (confirmed). So yes, server-side 400ms in those handlers.

Let me enumerate the RPCs in viewCartHandler (v0.10.3) precisely:
```go
currencies, err := fe.getCurrencies(ctx)
cart, err := fe.getCart(ctx, sessionID)
recommendations, err := fe.getRecommendations(ctx, sessionID, cartIDs)   // ← rec
type cartItemView...
for _, item := range cart { p, err := fe.getProduct(ctx, item.GetProductId()) ... }
shippingCost, err := fe.getShippingQuote(ctx, cart, currentCurrency)  // shipping
for ... convertCurrency
totalPrice, err := fe.convertCurrency(...)
```
And productHandler:
```go
p, err := fe.getProduct(ctx, id)
currencies, err := fe.getCurrencies(ctx)
cart, err := fe.getCart(ctx)
price, err := fe.convertCurrency(ctx, p.GetPriceUsd(), cur)
recommendations, err := fe.getRecommendations(ctx, sessionID, []string{id})  // ← rec
```
Home:
```go
currencies, getProducts, getCart, convertCurrency xN, chooseAd
```

So rec is the only common extra. And POST /cart (addToCart, 1ms) confirms product/cart/currency are fast.

So: EITHER the rec RPC takes ~400ms (my read) OR the frontend's calls to productcatalog/currency inside these handlers are slow *in these specific handlers* (impossible).

=> The rec RPC takes ~400ms. And rec receives it immediately, so the delay is inside rec (processing or its catalog call), or in the response path (rec→frontend).

Since ingress is fast, egress from rec (response) might be delayed... If netem delay were applied to the rec pod with 400ms *egress*, incoming requests would arrive immediately (matches!), the response would be delayed by 400ms (page +400ms ✓), AND the rec's own ListProducts call to catalog would also be delayed 400ms (ingress to catalog ... egress delay applies to rec's outbound packets: SYN/request delayed 400ms) — then rec's internal processing would be ~400 + then response +400 = 800ms total. Page = 400ms only, so no: rec's catalog call must be <50ms. So egress delay alone doesn't fit either (would add 800ms).

So: the delay is ~400ms once, on the response path OR inside processing.

If it's inside processing (after catalog call), then it's CPU/compute — but CPU limit 1 didn't help. Unless the pod's CPU is being *starved by the node*...

Let's check node capacity/allocation! I can't list nodes (forbidden). Hmm. But maybe I can see... no.

Hmm, what about "requests" of 100m: if the node has N CPUs and is over-committed, CFS shares... The pod *requests* 100m; when the node is contended, the pod is entitled to 100m/allocatable. If the node has 4 CPUs and 12 pods requesting ~1.5 CPU total, contention is low.

Hmm, but what if the same node is running the loadgenerator (Locust, 300m request) plus python... 

OK: If rec is CPU-starved, a 400ms stall for a trivial Python request implies severe starvation (40x slower than normal ~10ms). Node-wide, that would affect other pods too (the Go frontend handlers at 11ms would be more like 40ms+).

I'll go with: the delay is a ~400ms stall attributable to the recommendationservice pod — network egress shaping or CPU starvation, neither directly fixable via the manifest ops. BUT, hmm, we must propose something.

Let me reconsider scaling: if the cause is *per-connection or per-pod network state*, a new pod (2 replicas) would serve ~half the requests fast? No—new pod would have the same node-level netem.

Hmm hm. Wait wait wait. NEW IDEA: What if there are pod-level **NetworkChaos-like iptables rules** (e.g., from a chaos framework) — irrelevant.

Let me look once more for an in-cluster config anomaly that I might have dismissed: the frontend `ENABLE_PROFILER: 0` — in demo, frontend has ENABLE_PROFILER... whatever.

Hmm, what about `PRODUCT_CATALOG_SERVICE_ADDR` for recommendationservice → "productcatalogservice:3550" ✓.

What about the rec deployment's `DISABLE_PROFILER: 1` ✓ (avoids OpenTelemetry profiler overhead).

OK here's a thought experiment: which single env var, if changed, would make recommendation slow? E.g. `PRODUCT_CATALOG_SERVICE_ADDR` pointing to a **wrong port that blackholes** → the rec's ListProducts call would hang until a deadline (no deadline → hang forever). Not 400ms.

What if the rec's PRODUCT_CATALOG_SERVICE_ADDR pointed to `productcatalogservice:3550` — correct.

What if the *frontend's* RECOMMENDATION_SERVICE_ADDR pointed to a wrong target that is slow? It's correct.

OK, alternative: maybe the fault is in **cartservice/redis** but only on the cart page... no, product page also slow.

Honestly, let me consider one more possibility: the **frontend** has *two* gRPC connections to recommendation... no.

Hmm, let me look at the timings once more: cart page 408-440ms; product page 382-435ms; home 11-38ms. And the recv-vs-start offsets were ±6ms, +32ms, -6ms, +2ms, -6ms. If the rec call happened at start+~20ms and rec took ~390ms, response at 410ms ≈ page end. ✓ consistent.

Now let me test if the rec response itself is what's delayed: total rec processing = 390ms. Given it makes ONE ListProducts call... 

Hmm, unless it makes **many** calls: maybe it calls ListProducts and then *GetProduct for each*? Actually the recommendation service in the demo: 
```python
cat_response = product_catalog_stub.ListProducts(empty_pb2.Empty())
product_ids = [x.id for x in cat_response.products]
filtered_products = [pid for pid in product_ids if pid not in request.product_ids]
filtered_products = random.sample(filtered_products, min(len(filtered_products), max_responses))
```
One call. ~5ms.

So 390ms unexplained by app logic → must be waiting.

Wait a moment! What if the *Python* service can't reach productcatalogservice and grpc retries with backoff for ~390ms?? E.g., the connection is in reconnect backoff; grpc-python with `wait_for_ready=False` would fail fast though (and the frontend would see an error). Page rendered recommendations? Unknown! If getRecommendations errored, frontend logs a warning. Not seen (but the warning may be outside the retained buffer... the frontend's 5781-line buffer truncated older lines, and the warning rate would be 1/s → we'd definitely see some). Hmm, unless the error is logged at Debug/info level? In frontend code: `log.WithField("error", err).Warn("failed to retrieve recommendations")`. So it'd show.

Unless the frontend's `getRecommendations` uses a **context with a 400ms timeout**?? Hmm! No.

Hmm, hmm. But what if the recommendation service's gRPC server is *rejecting* connections and the client retries, and after ~400ms the RPC succeeds on a new connection? YES! That could fit: the frontend's half-open connection to the rec pod (dead after the pod was recreated at 17:01:04)... 

Hold on: THE REC POD WAS RECREATED at 17:01:04, and the *frontend pod* (16:55:21) has a long-lived gRPC connection to the rec Service ClusterIP. After the pod recreation, that connection is dead. gRPC detects the broken connection (TCP RST when new pod... hmm, the old pod is gone; packets to the old pod IP get no RST → the connection is half-open (blackholed), gRPC doesn't notice until TCP retransmit timeout (~1s+) or the RPC times out.

With a half-open connection, gRPC Go would: send the RPC on the dead connection, wait; TCP retransmits (initial RTO ~200ms, doubling: 200, 400, 800...). Eventually the connection fails → gRPC reconnects and *retries the RPC* only if the call is retryable/transparent retry... 

This ~400ms "first retransmit" pattern fits a half-open TCP connection! But after the connection recovers, subsequent RPCs are fast — we see +400ms on EVERY cart/product request for minutes. Unless the *frontend's* channel keeps alternating between a "dead" and "live" subchannel... there's only one.

Hmm, but you know what fits the +400ms CONSTANT on *all* rec calls over 5+ minutes? Something with **DNS**: the Go frontend resolved "recommendationservice" → ClusterIP at startup; each rec RPC goes to the ClusterIP. No per-RPC DNS.

Hmm! Unless... the frontend uses `grpc.WithBlock` dialing and the address is a Service; fine.

OK, radical idea: maybe the 400ms is spent in the *cart page's shipping quote* (cart) and *ads* (product)... and the common cause is something else entirely: **the frontend's sequential RPC count**? No, home has more.

Screw it. Let me look at the ACTUAL frontend source expectations vs this deployment's version: v0.10.3. Is there any chance the product page calls `getRecommendations` with the **whole product catalog** as product_ids? Hmm, no.

DECISION: I'll go with recommendationservice as the root cause and try the strongest available levers, plus one diagnostic that cleanly isolates it:

Actions (max 6):
1. `scale recommendationservice 2` — a second, fresh replica; halves load per pod; if the fault is pod-local (network/conntrack state of the old pod), roughly half of the rec calls get fast and latency drops.
2. `restart recommendationservice`? Conflicts with scale (scale alone creates a new pod; the old stays). Scaling to 2 then restarting would recreate both. Hmm, maybe scale to 2 is enough of a diagnostic: if latency halves → per-pod issue → scale to 3 helps. If nothing changes → it's not the rec pod.

Alternatively, isolate via the frontend: `unset_env frontend RECOMMENDATION_SERVICE_ADDR`?? That disables recommendations (frontend won't call rec; pages render without recs). If /cart & /product drop to <180ms, we've *proven* the rec path is the 400ms and — importantly — it's also a "fix" of the latency (at cost of a degraded feature).
